rationale: A2.3G requires determining possible solutions within a system's solution set. Fidelity V2 uses the secure Systems Workspace analyze mode so students must classify a marked point against every inequality and then supply an independently feasible ordered pair, while A2.3F remains responsible for constructing the full region.

documents.prompt: Use the displayed solution region for $y\ge {{m1}}x{{b1|signed}}$ and $y\le {{m2}}x{{b2|signed}}$. Decide whether the marked point is a possible solution, then enter a feasible ordered pair from the solution set.

solutionReview.headline: A possible solution must satisfy every inequality.
reasoning: At x=0, the marked y-value {{testY}} is above or on the lower boundary {{b1}}.
It is also below or on the upper boundary {{b2}}.
So the marked point belongs to the overlap.
solutionReview.answerSummary: The marked point is feasible; any second point in the overlap is also a possible solution.

attemptFeedback: Check the marked point against both inequalities, not only the one whose boundary is closest.
supportHints: A system means AND: every inequality must be true.

documents.prompt: The system is $y>{{m1}}x{{b1|signed}}$ and $y\le {{m2}}x{{b2|signed}}$. The marked point lies exactly on the dashed first boundary. Determine whether it is possible, then enter a feasible ordered pair from the solution set.

solutionReview.headline: A point on a strict boundary is not included.
reasoning: The first inequality uses >, so equality is not allowed.
At x=0 the marked point has y={{b1}}, exactly the first boundary value.
Therefore the marked point is not a possible solution even if it satisfies the second inequality.
solutionReview.answerSummary: Reject the marked boundary point; choose a point strictly above the first line and at/below the second.

attemptFeedback: A dashed boundary is excluded from the solution set.
supportHints: For > or <, a point exactly on the boundary fails that inequality.

documents.prompt: Determine whether the marked point is possible for ALL THREE constraints $y\ge {{m1}}x{{b1|signed}}$, $y\le {{m2}}x{{b2|signed}}$, and $y>{{floor}}$. then enter a feasible ordered pair from the solution set.

context.title: Three simultaneous restrictions
context.note: The point must satisfy every boundary condition at once.

solutionReview.headline: Three constraints still use one logical AND.
reasoning: At x=0 the marked point is above the first lower boundary.
It is below the upper boundary.
It is also strictly above y={{floor}}, so it survives all three constraints.
solutionReview.answerSummary: The marked point is feasible; another point in the three-way overlap is also possible.

attemptFeedback: Do not stop after two checks; a three-inequality system requires all three comparisons.
supportHints: A point failing even one inequality is outside the solution set.

documents.prompt: A planning model uses $y\ge0$, $y\ge x-{{shift}}$, and $y\le -x+{{cap}}$. Decide whether the marked plan is possible, then enter a feasible plan that satisfies all three constraints.

context.title: Feasible planning region
context.note: A marked plan is possible only when all three policy constraints hold.

solutionReview.headline: One violated planning constraint makes the marked plan impossible.
reasoning: At x={{testX}}, the lower sloped requirement is y≥{{requiredY}}.
Because the marked point has y=0<{{requiredY}}, it is not feasible.
solutionReview.answerSummary: Reject the marked plan; choose another point in the displayed overlap.

attemptFeedback: Use the actual marked coordinates in each policy inequality before deciding.
supportHints: A point can satisfy two constraints and still fail the system because of the third.

documents.prompt: A student says the marked point cannot be a solution because it lies on the boundary of $y\ge {{m1}}x{{b1|signed}}$. The full system is $y\ge {{m1}}x{{b1|signed}}$ and $y<{{m2}}x{{b2|signed}}$. Correct the student's decision, then enter a feasible point from the solution set.

context.title: Error analysis
context.note: Boundary inclusion depends on the inequality symbol, and the point must still satisfy the second constraint.

solutionReview.headline: Inclusive boundaries can contain valid system solutions.
reasoning: The ≥ symbol includes equality, so lying on the first boundary does not disqualify the point.
At x=0, the marked y-value {{b1}} is strictly below the second boundary value {{b2}}.
Therefore the marked point satisfies both inequalities.
solutionReview.answerSummary: The marked point is feasible; the student's boundary rule was wrong.

attemptFeedback: Do not use the blanket rule 'boundary points are never solutions.' Read the symbol.
supportHints: ≥ and ≤ include the boundary; > and < exclude it.
